newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief cautiously welcomes Clinton budget.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief cautiously welcomes Clinton budget.

text.p: Cautiously welcoming President Clinton's budget proposal for the United Nations, Secretary-General Kofi Annan called it a good faith effort to face the crippling effect of American debts on the world body.
"In principle the secretary-general has to say that he expects every member state to pay in full and on time," his spokesman Fred Eckhard told reporters.

"In practice, he can live with this compromise, which is of course, not consistent with the rules but represents, a good faith effort by the United States to come to terms with its arrears situation which is crippling the organization."

Clinton proposed to pay $1.02 billion in arrears for international organizations, of which $964 is for the United Nations. Some $100 million was to be appropriated this year, with the remainder approved but held until 1999, depending on reform measures instituted by the United Nations.

While the figures are certain to run into congressional opposition, they fall short of the $1.5 billion the United Nations says Washington owes. This includes $377 million for regular dues, $926 million for peacekeeping and $264 million for mandatory payments to several U.N. agencies.

The discrepancy, according to U.S. and U.N. officials, is mainly because of a unilateral decision by Congress in 1995 to lower peacekeeping costs, which accounts for a lower U.S. estimate of $268 plus withholding some 154 million for certain programs over the years.
The numbers also differ because of a $169 payment in regular dues Congress appropriated last year but which has not yet reached the United Nations, the U.S. officials said.

Marc Thiessen, a spokesman for Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which has to authorize the appropriation, said he expected "quibbling about the figures."
But he said Helms, a fierce critic of the United Nations, "was willing to pay the arrears as long as they are tied to benchmarks" that set out the pace of U.N. reforms.

The benchmarks will be set out in proposed legislation in the next month or so, with come committee staffers intending to travel to New York shortly to talk to Annan's staff about the draft legislation.
But the so-called "benchmarks" which might allow Washington to set the pace of reform bother Annan.

"U.S. benchmarks for payment are something he's uncomfortable with," Eckhard said. "What he proposes to the United States is that they accept the reform package that he will put on the table in mid to late summer, which he will develop in consultation with all 185 member states.

"That will be a quantifiable reform package and it will have a timetable attached to it. And so what he is saying is if you want to judge me by this reform package and my own timetable, then that's fine," Eckhard said.
